common_name: Golden King Aucuba (Male Pollinator with Heavy Gold-Blotched Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Golden King is a male selection, so it produces no berries itself but is an excellent pollinator for nearby female Aucuba cultivars such as 'Variegata' or 'Crotonifolia'.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade; direct sun bleaches and scorches the gold variegation. Golden King is one of the most heavily variegated Aucuba selections, with large, glossy, dark green leaves so densely blotched and splashed with golden-yellow that the foliage reads almost entirely gold at a distance, brightening dim corners of the garden year-round. As a male clone it never sets fruit, but its dense, rounded, slow-growing habit makes it a strong stand-alone specimen or hedge shrub for shade even without a pollination role, and its heavy pollen load ensures reliable berry set on any nearby female Aucuba within 30-40 feet. It tolerates salt spray, urban pollution, and heavy root competition under mature trees better than most broadleaf evergreens.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to deep shade; Limbata is a female cultivar introduced in the 19th century and remains uncommon in the trade due to slow growth, so plant a male Aucuba such as 'Mr. Goldstrike' or 'Golden King' nearby for berry set.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade, where the variegation is brightest and safest from leaf scorch. Limbata bears dark, glossy, deeply toothed evergreen leaves edged in a wide yellow border that pales to cream-white as the foliage ages, giving the shrub a refined, hand-painted look distinct from the speckled gold-dust type cultivars. It is a slow-growing, compact selection well suited to foundation plantings and woodland borders where a smaller-scale Aucuba is wanted, and as a female clone it sets attractive red berries in fall and winter when pollinated. This older heirloom selection is still uncommon in the nursery trade because of its slow propagation rate, but performs reliably once established in a shaded, sheltered site.

common_name: Lucky Leu Leucothoe (Peach-Orange New Growth Coastal Doghobble)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Lucky Leu tolerates more sun than many leucothoe selections but colors and performs best with afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; a patented Bailey Nurseries introduction of the native coastal doghobble, selected for its naturally full, mounded, low-maintenance habit that needs little pruning to stay dense and tidy. New growth emerges a striking peach-orange before maturing to glossy medium green, giving the evergreen shrub strong seasonal color on top of the small, fragrant, white urn-shaped spring flowers typical of the species. It is notably deer-resistant and tolerates damp, poorly drained soils better than many broadleaf evergreens, making it useful along shaded drainage areas and woodland edges. Mulch with pine bark or pine needles to help maintain the strongly acidic soil this native shrub prefers.

common_name: Ralph Shugert Periwinkle (White-Edged Variegated Vinca Minor)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions 12-18 inches apart in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Ralph Shugert spreads less aggressively than the plain species, making it a manageable choice near cultivated beds.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Ralph Shugert is an award-winning variegated selection of lesser periwinkle, bearing glossy dark green leaves edged in a narrow, uniform white margin that brightens shaded ground more effectively than the plain species without the strong color shift of gold-centered types. Large violet-blue pinwheel flowers appear from mid-spring into early summer above the trailing, node-rooting stems, which knit together into a dense, weed-suppressing evergreen mat. It is noticeably less vigorous and less prone to wandering into naturalized areas than straight Vinca minor, making it a better-behaved option for foundation plantings and small shaded beds. Shear lightly in early spring to remove winter-damaged foliage and encourage dense new growth.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions 12-18 inches apart in spring or fall in almost any well-drained soil in partial to full shade; stems root wherever they touch soil, filling gaps quickly once established.

directions: Plant in almost any soil in partial to deep shade; like the species, White Periwinkle tolerates dry shade under mature trees once established and needs essentially no maintenance beyond an occasional shearing to keep it dense. This is a classic white-flowered form of lesser periwinkle, producing the same small, glossy, dark evergreen leaves and trailing, mat-forming habit as the species but with crisp white, five-petaled pinwheel flowers instead of periwinkle-blue, giving a cooler, brighter look in shaded borders and woodland edges. Bloom is heaviest in spring with scattered rebloom through summer into fall. As with all Vinca minor, monitor spread near natural areas and remove any stray green-flowered seedlings to keep the planting true to type.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants 6-9 inches apart in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial to full shade; Silver Beauty is a slower spreader than green- or bronze-leaved ajuga cultivars, so allow extra time to fill in.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full shade; Silver Beauty bears soft grey-green leaves irregularly edged in creamy white, a subtler, cooler-toned variegation than the tricolor or near-black ajuga selections, useful for lightening dim corners without the visual weight of darker cultivars. Short spikes of blue flowers rise just above the foliage in late spring, drawing early bees. It spreads by surface stolons but more slowly than vigorous cultivars like 'Black Scallop', so it is a good choice for small-scale edging, rock gardens, and dry shade under trees where a slower, more contained groundcover is wanted. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and the clarity of the variegated foliage.
